claims.claim: Conflict resolution is defined in this lesson by Wikipedia's working definition — the methods and processes involved in facilitating the peaceful ending of conflict — which is corroborated by Kilmann Diagnostics' statement that conflict is a natural part of our interactions with others.

The Thomas-Kilmann tradition, from the TKI instrument published since 1974 by Kenneth W. Thomas and Ralph H. Kilmann, describes conflict behavior along two dimensions: assertiveness (how much a person tries to satisfy their own concerns) and cooperativeness (how much a person tries to satisfy the other person's concerns).

The five conflict-handling modes are competing (assertive, uncooperative, power-oriented), accommodating (unassertive, cooperative, self-sacrificing), avoiding (unassertive, uncooperative, sidestepping or postponing), collaborating (assertive and cooperative, digging into underlying needs and wants), and compromising (moderate in both, splitting the difference).

Every person is capable of using all five conflict-handling modes, and each mode is useful in some situations: Kilmann Diagnostics states that no mode is inherently right or wrong and that each of us is capable of using all five, and Wikipedia notes that not every style leads to an acceptable result in every situation.

A position is the specific demand a person states, while an interest is the underlying need the demand protects; Wikipedia's conflict-resolution treatment highlights an interest-based approach in which parties ask what each side actually needs rather than hammering the stated positions.

Organizations address conflict through defined processes: OpenStax Introduction to Business 8.8 describes grievance procedures (a formal complaint that management violated the contract, moving step by step from employee to supervisor to written documentation to higher-level meetings) and arbitration (settling a dispute through a third party whose decision is final and binding), with strikes and lockouts as pressure tactics when contracts expire.

The lesson's five-step resolution sequence — identify the issue, listen, discuss options, agree, and follow up — is a teaching synthesis presented in the spirit of structured conflict processes; its shape (define the issue, hear both sides, decide, confirm) matches the grievance and arbitration processes described in OpenStax Introduction to Business 8.8 and the peaceful-ending emphasis of Wikipedia's working definition.

Conflict can improve decisions: the lesson frames disagreement as a way to test weak ideas, and the goal of resolution is a peaceful ending both sides can live with rather than a victory — a framing consistent with the working definition's emphasis on facilitating a peaceful ending.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether any single conflict-handling style is best
positions: Popular advice often presents collaborating (win-win) as the ideal mode and the other four as inferior.
Kilmann Diagnostics states that each of the five modes is useful in some situations, that no mode is inherently right or wrong, and that each of us is capable of using all five.
Wikipedia notes that not every style leads to an acceptable result in every situation, so the choice depends on the circumstances.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the source consensus: the five modes are situational tools, not a ranking. It avoids claiming any mode is best, presents collaborating as valuable but time-intensive, and stresses choosing deliberately per situation.

sourceRecords.title: Overview of the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B but canonical: published by Dr. Ralph Kilmann, co-creator of the TKI. The live site blocks direct HTTP fetches; read via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20260608135557/ of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: the five conflict-handling modes — competing (assertive, uncooperative, power-oriented, standing up for your rights), accommodating (unassertive, cooperative, self-sacrificing, yielding), avoiding (unassertive, uncooperative, sidestepping, postponing, or withdrawing), collaborating (assertive AND cooperative, digging into the underlying needs and wants of both parties), compromising (moderate in both, splitting the difference); the two dimensions — assertiveness (satisfying your own concerns) and cooperativeness (satisfying the other person's concerns); the TKI published since 1974 by Kenneth W. Thomas and Ralph H. Kilmann; 'conflict is a natural part of our interactions with others'; each of us is capable of using all five modes; each mode is useful in some situations, so no mode is inherently right or wrong. Commercial site: paraphrase only, attribute to the Thomas-Kilmann tradition.
